Optimization chooses parameters to improve a scalar objective.
This note connects ordinary derivatives to parameter updates, then defines a supporting slope that remains meaningful for a convex objective at a corner.

## The update rule {#gradient-descent}

Let $L$ be the differentiable scalar objective being minimised, such as an [empirical risk](../machine-learning/loss.qmd#loss-and-risk).
For one real parameter, gradient descent repeatedly updates the parameter by subtracting a positive multiple of the objective's derivative:

$$
  w_{\text{new}}=w_{\text{old}}-\eta L'(w_{\text{old}}).
$$

The learning rate $\eta>0$ controls the step size.
A positive derivative gives a decrease in $w$; a negative derivative gives an increase.
The loss value measures the current penalty, while its derivative measures the local rate at which that penalty changes with the parameter.

For a differentiable objective $L:\mathbb R^d\rightarrow\mathbb R$, the gradient is the vector of its partial derivatives:

$$
  \nabla L(\mathbf w)=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}\\
  \vdots\\
  \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_d}
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Here, $\mathbf w$ contains the $d$ model parameters.
A partial derivative measures how the objective changes with one parameter while the other parameters are held fixed.
The vector update is $\mathbf w_{\text{new}}=\mathbf w_{\text{old}}-\eta\nabla L(\mathbf w_{\text{old}})$.

An excessive step can overshoot, increase the objective, or cause oscillation.
Moving opposite the gradient does not guarantee improvement for an arbitrary step size.
Training minimises the aggregate objective, so a step that improves it can still worsen an individual example.
For differentiable individual losses, the gradient of their average is the average of their gradients.
Examples can favour opposite changes, and their gradients can cancel while their errors remain nonzero.

## Definition and absolute-loss example {#subgradients}

Absolute loss has no ordinary derivative at zero.
For a convex function $\ell:\mathbb R\rightarrow\mathbb R$, a subgradient at $e$ is a number $g$ satisfying

$$
  \ell(z)\geq\ell(e)+g(z-e)
  \quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb R.
$$

Here, $e$ is the fixed point being examined, while $z$ ranges over all possible inputs.
Geometrically, $g$ is the slope of a line through $(e,\ell(e))$ that never rises above the function's graph.
This criterion still applies when there is no unique tangent slope.

For $\ell(e)=|e|$, the set of valid subgradients at zero is

$$
  \partial\ell(0)=[-1,1].
$$

A subgradient is one number $g$; the subdifferential $\partial\ell(0)$ is the set of all valid subgradients.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false" title="Proof: the subdifferential of absolute loss at zero"}

At $e=0$, the subgradient condition becomes

$$
  |z|\geq gz
  \quad\text{for every real }z.
$$

For $z>0$, this requires $z\geq gz$, hence $g\leq1$.
For $z<0$, it requires $-z\geq gz$.
Dividing by negative $z$ reverses the inequality, giving $g\geq-1$.
At $z=0$, the inequality holds automatically.
Together, these conditions are necessary and sufficient for $g\in[-1,1]$.

:::

## Connections {#connections}

[Loss and empirical risk](../machine-learning/loss.qmd#loss-and-risk) defines common objectives and derives the minimisers of squared and absolute error.
[Stop-gradient](../computer-software/stop-gradient.qmd) changes which paths contribute to an update without changing the forward value.
[Exponential moving averages](exponential-moving-average.qmd) can average model parameters across updates; the averaged object must be specified.
